newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Three dissidents to leave HK soon, more remain.
newsitem.headline: Three dissidents to leave HK soon, more remain.

text.p: Three mainland dissidents stranded in Hong Kong in the waning days of British rule will leave for sanctuary in Sweden or Denmark before the territory's handover on July 1, a dissidents' support group said on Friday.

Another three have yet to decide whether to stay on after Britain hands back Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30, said Lu Siqing, spokesman for the Information Centre of Human Rights and the Democratic Movement in China.

The six are the last of hundreds of people, mainly students, who fled to western countries via Hong Kong in the wake of China's bloody military crackdown in 1989 on a pro-democracy movement centred in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Many dissidents worried they would be harassed if they stayed in Hong Kong after China takes control of the territory.

Six dissidents left for western countries this week under refugee status granted by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), with the help of a "document of identity" (DI) from the Hong Kong colonial government, Lu said.
"If they get DI, they can stay in Hong Kong as a resident or go to other countries that offer them visas," he told Reuters.
Britain took in three of the dissidents who fled over the last four days, Sweden took two and Denmark one.
Chen Ziying, Zhang Junzhong and Zhang Taisong would leave the territory on either Friday night or Saturday, Lu said.

Zhang Taisong had threatened to set himself on fire at an annual candlelit vigil commemorating the June 4, 1989, crackdown in a bid to force the Hong Kong government to speed the exit of remaining dissidents.

"There are only three who may still be here before the handover," Lu said. "I have lost contact with one of them and the other two are still considering whether to go or stay, but they have DIs from the Hong Kong government already."
If no country granted visas to the last three dissidents, they could apply for refugee status at the UNHCR, allowing them to leave freely after the handover, he said.

Lu told a local newspaper on Friday that if outgoing colonial Governor Chris Patten wanted to keep his promise to help the stranded dissidents, he should send them to Britain within the next few days because other countries might not accept them.

The remaining dissidents have said they do not intend to protest during the handover ceremony on the night of June 30, which will be attended by Chinese President Jiang Zemin, Britain's Prince Charles and Prime Minister Tony Blair, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and 4,000 other VIPs.
